memoryText: My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Psalm 73:26 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is the climax of Psalm 73, written by a man who almost lost his faith. After all his struggles, he comes to this confession.

“My flesh and my heart may fail.” He is honest about his limits. Flesh is the body, with its weakness and mortality. Heart is the inner life, with its feelings and strength. Both can fail. The prosperous wicked looked so strong, and the psalmist felt so weak. But he does not say that his flesh and heart will not fail. They may. He admits it.

“But God is the strength of my heart.” The word for strength can mean rock. God is the rock of my heart. When all else gives way, he is solid. Notice the difference: it is not that I am strong, but that God is my strength. The psalmist did not discover an inner reserve of courage. He discovered that God holds him up.

“And my portion forever.” A portion was a share of inheritance. In the land of Israel, each family received a portion. The Levites received none, because the LORD was their portion. The psalmist makes this his own. He says that God is his inheritance. Everything else may be lost, but God is his share. And it is forever, beyond death.

This is a verse for the weak and the weary. It does not ask you to be strong. It invites you to rest your weakness on the one who is. Say this verse when your body is tired, when your heart is troubled, or when you fear the future. God is the strength of your heart, and he is your portion forever.
weekInReview: This week you prayed two psalms of crisis: Psalm 73, where Asaph nearly stumbled when he saw the prosperity of the wicked until he entered God’s presence and declared, “Whom have I in heaven but you?”, and Psalm 77, where God’s footprints were unseen but his way was holy. You walked through the first part of Ezekiel. You saw the prophet act out the siege of Jerusalem, and watched the idolatry in the temple in his vision. You watched the glory of the LORD depart from the temple in reluctant stages, and heard the promise of a heart of flesh and a new spirit. You read God’s warnings against false prophets who whitewash a weak wall, and against idols in the heart. And you read the parables of the useless vine, the faithless wife, and the cedar sprig, which ended with an everlasting covenant. The week taught that God takes sin seriously, that his glory is not confined to a building, and that he promises a new heart.
reflectionQuestions: Asaph’s view changed when he entered God’s presence. What would it look like to bring a question or envy into God’s presence this week, and wait?
Ezekiel saw the glory of God leave the temple, and then promised a heart of flesh. What hardness in your heart do you most need God to soften?
God says “Live!” to the abandoned child in chapter 16. How does this image of grace shape how you understand your own story?
prayerPrompts: Tell God what is failing in you, and tell him he is the strength of your heart.
Thank him for the new heart he has promised.
